passage:
The summer I turned twelve, my parents sent me to spend July with my great-aunt Hedda in Callow Bend, a river town with two churches, one traffic light, and a hardware store that also sold bait. I had met Hedda only twice, both times at funerals, and I expected a month of silence and boiled vegetables. She had retired the spring before. For thirty-eight years she had worked the night ward at the county hospital, and half the town had been born or stitched up under her watch.

Her house was narrow and dim, with a porch that sagged toward the road. Hedda kept a dozen hens in a wire run behind the house and could tell each one apart by the sound of its complaints. On the first evening I noticed a framed photograph on the mantel, the only picture in the room, and Hedda caught me looking at it. 'People could never tell us apart,' she said, 'except that she was always the one laughing at something.'

Callow Bend sits where the river turns hard to the east, and the water there runs deep and fast. A ferry had once crossed at the bend, but it had stopped running before I was born. When the crossing trade went, it took half of Front Street with it, and the shops there had stood empty ever since.

What filled that July, though, was a crate of water-stained books from the church cellar. She showed me how to lift a ruined spine, sew the loose pages back into their bundles, and glue fresh cloth over the boards. By my last day we had saved forty-one of them, and she let me write my name inside the cover of the last.

When I think now of the twelve-year-old who arrived in Callow Bend expecting boiled vegetables, I want to sit beside that child and promise that it will all be fine. Being handed to a near stranger is frightening at any age, and that gloomy forecast was only fear in disguise.

passage:
Tarrow Marsh is a mile of mudflat, creek and cordgrass on a quiet coast, and it is the only known home of the banded marsh crab, an animal no wider than a thumbnail. The species was first described in 1897 by the doctor of a supply ship anchored off the marsh, who sketched it in his medical log. Each summer the flats swarm with the crabs. Each October they disappear, and for more than a century nobody could say where they went.

The storm of 1953 is remembered at Tarrow for one lasting change: it breached the old sea dike in four places, and the dike was rebuilt a full yard higher, as the wall that still guards the fields behind the marsh. During the long search for the crabs, researchers worked from the marsh's field station, a small hut at the landward edge. Its one diesel generator ran only between dusk and midnight, so late notes were written by lamplight.

The search began in earnest in 2016, when the ecologist Peter Halloran and his team glued tiny numbered tags to two hundred crabs each September. For three winters the tagged animals simply vanished. In the fourth, the team found them in the reed beds at the marsh's upper edge. Every tagged crab they recovered had wedged itself inside the hollow stem of a dead reed, one crab to a stem, well above the reach of the winter tides. After more than a century, the crabs' winter hiding place was finally known.

Much of the fieldwork in those winters fell to Mara Sollis, who had joined the project as an unpaid volunteer when she retired at sixty. Forty years of fitting hairsprings and balance wheels at a jeweler's bench had given her the steadiest hands on the team. Halloran still calls her the best recruit the project ever had.

Halloran's team is now planning a fifth winter on the flats. Few researchers would have spent four freezing winters chasing an animal the size of a thumbnail, and such patience deserves to be held up as a model.
